evidence_quotes.quote: More recently the trend has been towards recovering other system development costs from communities, including capital costs. Cost recovery is now an important part of any project implementation process, and it is often credited with beneficial side effects such as enhancing system sustainability, or community capacity-building.
Communities that are unwilling or unable to do so may have to wait until government resources become available or until the community gathers sufficient resources itself.

The issues discussed in this paper are the result of an inquiry over the past four years into the training and capacity building of community-based institutions so that they may manage improved water and sanitation resources.

criterion_notes.c1: Focuses on the provision, financing, affordability, and sustainability of community water supply and household sanitation facilities in rural and peri-urban communities in developing countries.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording, it examines institutional, financial, and governance arrangements for community water and sanitation delivery. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it specifically examines cost-recovery rules, community self-financing mandates, loan/debt repayment obligations, and subsidy/affordability criteria directly governing whether poor communities obtain and sustain water and sanitation services (falling squarely within tariff or cost-recovery rules). Exclusion is due to Criterion 3 (no empirical evidence), so both the narrow and plain Criterion 2 full-text decisions are exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Does not contain primary empirical data, an identifiable empirical research method, or a systematic empirical synthesis. It is a policy commentary/essay critiquing donor cost-recovery and community self-financing strategies and proposing five conceptual steps for sector policy, citing a few secondary reports only as brief illustrative examples. Excluded under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: Discusses coverage, affordability, delays in obtaining water systems, and system sustainability conceptually, but reports no empirical outcome measurements or primary/synthesized outcome data.
criterion_notes.c5: Because the paper is a non-empirical policy essay, there is no identifiable empirical study design, sample, measured exposure, or measured outcome.

country: Developing nations generally (non-empirical policy essay briefly citing secondary examples in Togo, Indonesia, and Nigeria)
exposure: Cost-recovery and community self-financing policies/requirements for water supply and sanitation systems (conceptual discussion only)
rationale: Full text matches metadata (Yacoob 1990, Health Policy and Planning). Although the paper addresses rural and peri-urban water supply and sanitation access (c1=yes) and directly examines cost-recovery, subsidy, and community self-financing rules governing service access under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (c2=yes), it is a non-empirical policy essay/commentary with no primary empirical data, no empirical study design, and no systematic synthesis methodology (c3=no). Accordingly, it is excluded under code E05 (No empirical evidence).
